headline: Get an RTX 5090 Alienware PC for less than the GPU alone with a $1,550 discount
summary: The Alienware Area-51 Gaming Desktop with an RTX 5090 is currently available for $4,779, making the entire system cheaper than the standalone graphics card.
details: You can now get an Alienware Area-51 Gaming Desktop featuring an RTX 5090 for $4,779, a $1,550 discount. This makes the entire PC cheaper than buying the RTX 5090 graphics card by itself, which currently costs at least $4,799 standalone.
The deal includes a 20-core Intel Ultra 7 265K processor, 32GB of DDR5 7200 RAM, a 1TB M.2 Gen 5 SSD, and a 1500W power supply. It also comes with Windows 11 and a 240mm AIO CPU cooler.
The RTX 5090 is a top-tier graphics card, boasting 32GB GDDR7 VRAM and 21,760 CUDA cores. It's designed to handle 4K gaming and demanding local AI workloads with ease.

While the Intel Core Ultra 7 265K CPU might seem slightly underpowered for this level, its strong single-threaded performance complements the RTX 5090. In testing, this pairing achieved an average of 150 FPS at 1080p across 17 games.

For those seeking a CPU boost, a Core Ultra 9 285 option is available. The system's DDR5 6400 RAM can be upgraded to DDR5 7200 with Intel 200S boost for free, potentially increasing gaming performance by 7%.
This deal offers exceptional value in the current PC market, where GPU prices continue to climb. Acquiring a full gaming rig for less than the cost of its flagship GPU is a rare opportunity.

headline: AI data center optical interconnect market to hit $144 billion by 2030, a 10x increase from 2024
summary: New projections show the market growing over tenfold from $13.7 billion in 2024. Silicon photonics, driven by co-packaged optics, is expected to capture nearly two-thirds of this revenue.
details: The global data center optical interconnect market is projected to reach $144.4 billion by 2030, a massive jump from $13.7 billion in 2024. This represents a 48.1% compound annual growth rate (CAGR), according to a report by China Insights Consultancy (CIC).

Silicon photonics is expected to drive this growth, accounting for 63.7% of the future market revenue. Its share is climbing from 16.6% in 2020 as the industry shifts towards denser, more power-efficient designs like co-packaged optics.

The AI industry has already invested over $15 billion in co-packaged optics, photonic chips, and higher-speed transceiver modules. This includes developing new integration techniques, acquiring photonics startups, and forming alliances among major players.

For decades, data centers relied on copper for data transfer, which is cheap and reliable. However, copper's power consumption and signal losses increase sharply with bandwidth and distance, hitting a wall for high-speed AI data centers.

The solution is a transition to photonics, moving data as light instead of electrical signals. Optical transceivers convert electrical signals to laser light, sending it down fiber for far more bandwidth over greater distances at higher speeds, pushing from 400G to 1.6T and beyond.

Co-packaged optics (CPO) aims to bring optics closer to the compute, placing the photonic integrated circuit (PIC) directly on the switch or accelerator package. This shrinks the electrical path to millimeters, significantly reducing power consumption at extreme data rates.

Laser chips, which are highly sensitive to heat, remain separate from the PIC, which becomes part of the hot switch or accelerator package. These laser chips are always needed, whether for CPO or pluggable modules.

Silicon Photonics (SiPh) enables patterning optical circuitry onto silicon using mature CMOS processes, making PICs mass-producible and cost-effective. However, silicon cannot generate light, so laser chips still rely on more expensive III-V materials.
